statement:
(i) Show that
$$\int_0^1\bigl(1+(\alpha-1)x\bigr)^n\,dx=\frac{\alpha^{n+1}-1}{(n+1)(\alpha-1)}$$
when $\alpha\neq 1$ and $n$ is a positive integer.

(ii) Show that if $0\le k\le n$ then the coefficient of $\alpha^k$ in the polynomial
$$\int_0^1\bigl(\alpha x+(1-x)\bigr)^n\,dx$$
is
$$\binom{n}{k}\int_0^1 x^k(1-x)^{n-k}\,dx.$$

(iii) Hence, or otherwise, show that
$$\int_0^1 x^k(1-x)^{n-k}\,dx=\frac{k!(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}.$$
solution:
(i) Substituting $u=1+(\alpha-1)x$, so $du=(\alpha-1)dx$:
$$\int_0^1\bigl(1+(\alpha-1)x\bigr)^n dx=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\int_{1}^{\alpha}u^n\,du=\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\left[\frac{u^{n+1}}{n+1}\right]_1^{\alpha}=\frac{\alpha^{n+1}-1}{(n+1)(\alpha-1)}.$$

(ii) Write $\alpha x+(1-x)=1+(\alpha-1)x$. By the binomial theorem,
$$\bigl(1+(\alpha-1)x\bigr)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}(\alpha-1)^k x^k.$$

Now $(\alpha-1)^k=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}\alpha^j(-1)^{k-j}$, so the coefficient of $\alpha^k$ in the whole expression comes from collecting terms. Alternatively, rewrite directly:
$$\bigl(\alpha x+(1-x)\bigr)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}(\alpha x)^k(1-x)^{n-k}.$$

This is the cleaner form: here the coefficient of $\alpha^k$ is $\binom{n}{k}x^k(1-x)^{n-k}$. Integrating term by term, the coefficient of $\alpha^k$ in the integral is
$$\binom{n}{k}\int_0^1 x^k(1-x)^{n-k}\,dx.$$

(iii) By (i), for $\alpha\neq 1$,
$$\int_0^1\bigl(1+(\alpha-1)x\bigr)^n dx=\frac{\alpha^{n+1}-1}{(n+1)(\alpha-1)}=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\alpha^j.$$

(using the geometric sum $\alpha^{n+1}-1=(\alpha-1)(1+\alpha+\cdots+\alpha^n)$).

Thus the coefficient of $\alpha^k$ (for $0\le k\le n$) is $\dfrac{1}{n+1}$, uniformly for each $k$. But by (ii) this coefficient equals $\binom{n}{k}\int_0^1 x^k(1-x)^{n-k}dx$. Hence
$$\binom{n}{k}\int_0^1 x^k(1-x)^{n-k}dx=\frac{1}{n+1},$$
so
$$\int_0^1 x^k(1-x)^{n-k}dx=\frac{1}{(n+1)\binom{n}{k}}=\frac{k!(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}.$$

as required.
hints: For (ii), expand (alpha x + (1-x))^n via the binomial theorem with terms (alpha x)^k (1-x)^{n-k}.
For (iii), rewrite the result of (i) using the geometric sum to read off the coefficient of alpha^k.
